rawInput.complaint:
A 61-year-old African-American man presented with a four-day history of binocular diplopia, left eyelid droop, and numbness and tingling in both hands and feet. He also reported one month of profound fatigue and progressive proximal weakness, to the point of being unable to ambulate. His medical history was notable for biopsy-proven sarcoidosis treated with steroids in 1970, gout, dyspepsia, and mild obstructive pulmonary disease. He had lost 30 pounds over six months and had a chronic dry cough.

On examination, vital signs were normal. Cranial-nerve testing revealed significant left eyelid ptosis (1 mm aperture), impaired adduction, abduction, and upward gaze bilaterally, partial right III and VI nerve palsies, and almost complete left III and VI nerve palsies. There was subtle bilateral facial weakness, decreased left facial sensation to pinprick, and proximal muscle atrophy with 4/5 strength in the shoulders and hips, 3/5 in lower extremities, preserved distal strength, decreased to absent reflexes bilaterally, and mildly decreased distal leg sensation. The abdomen was diffusely mildly tender; joints were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 10.9 g/dL, normal calcium, electrolytes, renal function, HIV serology, vitamin B12, folate, muscle enzymes, and infectious serologies except mildly elevated AST and total bilirubin. ESR was 66 mm/hr, CRP normal, and urinalysis revealed 3+ proteinuria (normal six months earlier). Head CT was normal.

He was treated with five days of IVIG for a presumed Guillain-Barré–like syndrome. Chest CT showed multiple calcified nodules (some larger than prior studies) and a new right lower lobe infiltrate. Brain MRI/MRA (including orbits with gadolinium) was unremarkable. Nerve conduction studies and EMG revealed a diffuse, predominantly axonal, length-dependent sensory-motor polyneuropathy with myopathic features. Lumbar MRI showed multilevel degeneration. CSF analysis demonstrated albuminocytologic dissociation (protein 105 mg/dL). CT abdomen and pelvis showed minimal free fluid. Fine-needle aspiration of the lung infiltrate showed inflammatory cells and plasma cells without granulomas; cultures were negative. Muscle biopsy showed inflammatory myopathy with fiber atrophy and regeneration without vasculitis. Sural nerve biopsy revealed no acute abnormality but evidence of possible old vasculitis.

cotDiagnosis.reasoning:
The chief complaint is a subacute neuromuscular syndrome with prominent cranial neuropathies: four days of binocular diplopia and left ptosis, plus distal paresthesias, superimposed on one month of profound fatigue and progressive proximal weakness severe enough to prevent ambulation. The patient’s broader concern is a systemic process, suggested by 30-pound weight loss over six months and chronic dry cough, in the setting of remote biopsy-proven sarcoidosis.

Salient positive findings strongly suggest a multisystem inflammatory disorder affecting muscle, peripheral nerve, and cranial nerves. Neurologically, he has bilateral ophthalmoplegia with partial right and near-complete left III and VI palsies, left ptosis, subtle bilateral facial weakness, decreased left facial sensation, proximal muscle atrophy and weakness (4/5 shoulders/hips, 3/5 lower extremities), preserved distal strength, decreased to absent reflexes, and mild distal sensory loss. Electrodiagnostics show a diffuse predominantly axonal length-dependent sensorimotor polyneuropathy with myopathic features, supporting combined neuropathic and myopathic involvement rather than a pure neuromuscular junction disorder. Muscle biopsy confirms inflammatory myopathy with fiber atrophy/regeneration. CSF protein is elevated to 105 mg/dL with albuminocytologic dissociation, which can occur in inflammatory neuropathies but is not specific. Systemically, ESR is elevated at 66 mm/hr, there is new 3+ proteinuria, anemia (hemoglobin 10.9 g/dL), weight loss, chronic cough, and chest CT abnormalities including multiple calcified nodules and a new right lower lobe infiltrate. Sural nerve biopsy did not show acute changes but did show possible old vasculitis. He also has a history of sarcoidosis, which raises the possibility of recurrence with neurologic and muscular involvement.

Pertinent negatives help narrow the differential. Brain MRI/MRA including orbits with gadolinium was unremarkable, arguing against a compressive, ischemic brainstem, cavernous sinus, or orbital apex lesion causing the multiple cranial neuropathies. Head CT was normal. Normal muscle enzymes make some inflammatory myopathies less obvious, but biopsy proves myositis despite normal enzymes. HIV, B12, folate, and infectious serologies were unrevealing, making infectious neuropathy/myopathy less likely. Calcium and renal function were normal, which does not support metabolic causes. Fine-needle aspiration of the lung infiltrate showed inflammatory cells/plasma cells without granulomas, so there was no tissue confirmation of active pulmonary sarcoid from that site. Joints were unremarkable, which makes a classic systemic rheumatologic vasculitis less clinically obvious, though not excluded.

The first major differential is neurosarcoidosis with sarcoid myopathy and peripheral neuropathy. This fits the remote biopsy-proven sarcoidosis, chronic cough, pulmonary nodules/infiltrate, weight loss, multiple cranial neuropathies (especially ophthalmoplegia and facial sensory/motor involvement), inflammatory myopathy on biopsy, and peripheral neuropathy. Sarcoidosis is well known to cause cranial neuropathies and can involve muscle and peripheral nerves. The normal MRI does not exclude neurosarcoidosis, especially cranial neuropathic disease. The elevated ESR and proteinuria are compatible with systemic inflammation. Against this diagnosis is the lack of granulomas on lung FNA and the sural nerve biopsy showing only possible old vasculitis rather than granulomatous inflammation, but sampling error is common and sarcoid can still be the unifying diagnosis.

A second differential is Guillain-Barré syndrome or a GBS variant such as Miller-Fisher overlap. Supporting features include subacute weakness, areflexia, sensory symptoms, cranial nerve involvement, and albuminocytologic dissociation. However, several findings argue against this as the primary diagnosis: the weakness had been progressive over a month with marked proximal atrophy, EMG showed axonal length-dependent polyneuropathy with myopathic features rather than a typical acute demyelinating process, muscle biopsy showed inflammatory myopathy, and the substantial systemic features (weight loss, cough, proteinuria, elevated ESR, pulmonary infiltrate/nodules) are not explained by GBS. The presumed GBS-like syndrome was therefore an understandable initial impression but does not best unify the case.

A third differential is systemic vasculitic neuropathy with inflammatory myopathy. This is supported by weight loss, elevated ESR, new proteinuria, neuropathy, cranial neuropathies, and sural nerve biopsy evidence of possible old vasculitis. Vasculitis can produce mononeuritis multiplex or axonal neuropathy and can involve muscle. However, the neuropathy was described as diffuse length-dependent rather than classic asymmetric mononeuritis multiplex, muscle biopsy showed no vasculitis, and the prior history of sarcoidosis plus pulmonary findings make sarcoidosis a more cohesive explanation. Vasculitis remains plausible, especially sarcoid-associated vasculitic change, but less likely as the primary standalone diagnosis.

Other considerations are less convincing. Myasthenia gravis could explain ptosis and ophthalmoplegia with preserved imaging, but it does not explain areflexia, sensory loss, axonal polyneuropathy, inflammatory myopathy on biopsy, CSF protein elevation, proteinuria, or systemic inflammatory/pulmonary findings. An isolated idiopathic inflammatory myopathy such as polymyositis would fit proximal weakness and biopsy findings, but would not explain the multiple cranial neuropathies and sensory-motor polyneuropathy. Paraneoplastic disease is conceivable given weight loss and lung infiltrate, but available pathology showed no malignancy and the known sarcoidosis history offers a stronger explanation.

Overall, the most likely diagnosis is recurrent systemic sarcoidosis with neurosarcoid involvement causing multiple cranial neuropathies, peripheral neuropathy, and sarcoid inflammatory myopathy. This diagnosis best integrates the prior biopsy-proven sarcoidosis, pulmonary abnormalities, constitutional symptoms, bilateral ophthalmoplegia/ptosis with other cranial nerve deficits, inflammatory myopathy on muscle biopsy, and mixed axonal neuropathy. The GBS-like features and possible old vasculitis are better viewed as overlapping manifestations within a broader sarcoid-related inflammatory neuropathy/myopathy syndrome rather than the primary diagnosis.

differentialDiagnoses.condition: Neurosarcoidosis with sarcoid myopathy and peripheral neuropathy
differentialDiagnoses.supportingEvidence: Remote biopsy-proven sarcoidosis, chronic cough and pulmonary nodules/infiltrate, weight loss, multiple cranial neuropathies (III, VI, facial/trigeminal involvement), inflammatory myopathy on muscle biopsy, and diffuse axonal sensorimotor polyneuropathy on EMG/NCS.

Subacute weakness, areflexia, sensory symptoms, ophthalmoplegia, facial weakness, and CSF albuminocytologic dissociation support an acute inflammatory neuropathy, but myopathic biopsy findings and systemic inflammatory/pulmonary features are not explained well.

differentialDiagnoses.condition: Systemic vasculitic neuropathy with inflammatory myopathy
differentialDiagnoses.supportingEvidence: Weight loss, ESR 66 mm/hr, new 3+ proteinuria, axonal neuropathy, cranial neuropathies, and sural nerve biopsy showing possible old vasculitis are supportive, but muscle biopsy lacked vasculitis and prior sarcoidosis provides a more unifying cause.
Ptosis and ophthalmoplegia fit, but sensory loss, areflexia, axonal polyneuropathy, inflammatory myopathy on biopsy, and systemic inflammatory findings argue strongly against it.
Proximal weakness and inflammatory myopathy on biopsy fit, but this would not account for the prominent multiple cranial neuropathies, sensory symptoms, areflexia, and axonal polyneuropathy.

cotDiagnosis.finalDiagnosis: Neurosarcoidosis with sarcoid myopathy and peripheral neuropathy
